column1: What is the formula relating wavelength, speed of sound, and frequency, and what is the speed of sound at sea level/20°C?
column2: λ = c/f, where c ≈ 343 m/s at sea level and 20°C. Wavelength and frequency are inversely coupled.

column1: Why does doubling a frequency always produce the perceptual interval of an octave, regardless of starting pitch?
column2: Pitch perception is logarithmic, not linear. 110→220 Hz and 440→880 Hz are both octaves because each semitone is a fixed ratio (12th root of 2 ≈ 1.05946), so equal perceptual steps correspond to equal frequency ratios, not equal frequency differences.

column1: What does 0 dBFS represent in digital audio, and where should a well-recorded vocal typically peak?
column2: 0 dBFS is the maximum possible digital amplitude before clipping; all levels are negative relative to it. A well-recorded vocal typically peaks between -6 dBFS and -3 dBFS to preserve headroom.

column1: What is the foundational invariant shared by additive, subtractive, and FM synthesis architectures?
column2: Musical timbre emerges from the time-varying spectral distribution of energy across the frequency spectrum; each architecture is a different computational strategy for sculpting that frequency domain.

column1: What is aliasing in digital oscillator design, and why do naive table-lookup/polynomial oscillators produce it?
column2: Aliasing is harsh, inharmonic distortion caused by frequencies above the Nyquist limit (half the sample rate) folding back into the audible spectrum. Naive oscillators lack bandlimiting, so harmonics of high-pitched, harmonically rich waveforms exceed Nyquist and fold back.

column1: Name two bandlimited oscillator techniques used to prevent aliasing in digital synthesis.
column2: BLEP (bandlimited step) and PolyBLEP (polynomial bandlimited step), or wavetable interpolation with proper reconstruction filtering.

column1: State the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem and its practical implication at 48 kHz sample rate.
column2: The sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency component to faithfully reconstruct a signal. At 48 kHz, frequencies up to 24 kHz are theoretically representable, but anti-aliasing filters practically roll off above ~20 kHz.

column1: How does filter Quality Factor (Q) affect frequency response, and what happens at extreme high Q?
column2: Low Q (0.5–1.0) gives a broad, gentle resonance peak suitable for musical tone shaping; high Q (10–100) creates a narrow, aggressive peak that can drive the filter into self-oscillation, turning it into a sine wave generator.

column1: What is a critical band, and how does its width change below vs. above 500 Hz?
column2: A critical band is a frequency range within which the ear cannot resolve individual spectral components. Below ~500 Hz it is roughly constant at 100 Hz wide; above 500 Hz it scales logarithmically at approximately one-third octave intervals.

column1: What is the mechanism behind auditory masking, and what is the difference between pre-masking and post-masking?
column2: Masking occurs when two signals share a critical band and the louder one raises the perceptual threshold for the quieter one. Pre-masking reduces sensitivity to sounds just before a loud transient; post-masking reduces sensitivity to sounds just after it. Perceptual codecs exploit this to save bits.

column1: According to Fletcher-Munson equal-loudness contours, where is human hearing most sensitive, and why?
column2: Peak sensitivity is centered around 3–4 kHz, corresponding to the resonant frequency of the ear canal itself; loudness perception is frequency-dependent, not just amplitude-dependent.

column1: What foundational mathematical principle, formalized by Fourier in 1822, underlies all signal processing and EQ operations?
column2: Any periodic or finite-duration signal can be expressed as a weighted sum of sine and cosine waves (the Fourier transform), meaning time-domain and frequency-domain representations are dual, complementary views of the same signal.
